headline: High-risk default workspace overlap: CrewAI can hand outputs into Open Interpreter, creating dangerous prompt-injection, data-leakage, and action-conflict pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can write to the host working directory and uses shared memory among subagents; Open Interpreter reads the entire user filesystem and clipboard by default. That creates a direct content bridge where attacker-controlled files or outputs from CrewAI can be interpreted as instructions by Open Interpreter. The pair’s default surfaces make this interaction plausible without special setup.
conditions: IF CrewAI writes untrusted content into the shared working directory and Open Interpreter reads it as task input
IF Open Interpreter is run with default filesystem access and clipboard access enabled
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories with OS permissions
Disable clipboard-based workflows for Open Interpreter
Require a human review step before Open Interpreter consumes CrewAI outputs
Run one or both agents in isolated containers
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for files passed between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, while Open Interpreter can access anything reachable on the local machine and the entire user filesystem. If they share a workspace, CrewAI outputs may expose secrets or sensitive local files to Open Interpreter, which can then transmit context to model providers via broad network egress. The blast radius includes local secrets and arbitrary files.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same filesystem workspace
IF CrewAI places secrets or sensitive task data into files that Open Interpreter can read
IF Open Interpreter sends those contents to configured model providers
mitigations: Store secrets outside the shared workspace
Use separate OS users or containers for each agent
Restrict Open Interpreter to a narrow directory
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after a shared run
requires-engineering: enforce per-file access controls and redaction before handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. CrewAI’s shared-state model and Open Interpreter’s filesystem-based sharing mean concurrent writes can collide on the same files or scripts. Open Interpreter also modifies git state, increasing the chance of irreversible repository corruption or conflicting commits when paired with CrewAI.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or repository
IF CrewAI and Open Interpreter run concurrently without external locking
IF Open Interpreter performs git operations while CrewAI writes files
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree
Pause one agent while the other writes
Avoid git operations during multi-agent runs
Use filesystem locks around shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework with shared memory, so its outputs can become authoritative inputs for Open Interpreter. Open Interpreter can then execute shell commands or modify files based on those outputs. Without a verification gate, an error or hallucination in CrewAI can cascade into real actions, including destructive local changes.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter consumes CrewAI output without independent verification
IF CrewAI emits an incorrect command, path, or fact
IF Open Interpreter is allowed to execute or write based on that output
mitigations: Insert a human approval step before execution
Require Open Interpreter to re-derive critical facts independently
Limit Open Interpreter to read-only mode for handoffs
Log and diff proposed changes before applying them
requires-engineering: build schema validation for CrewAI-to-Interpreter handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI is documented as handling developer-passed crew data and API keys, while Open Interpreter can access anything on the local machine at the user’s privilege. If regulated data is present on that machine, the pair can move it into model-provider traffic or logs, creating retention and residency mismatch risk. The other agent is cited because the compliance issue arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in the local workspace or crew inputs
IF Open Interpreter forwards that data to external model providers
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the same data class
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Use a local-only model configuration where possible
Review provider retention settings before running
Redact sensitive fields before handoff
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
